title: A Practical Guide to File Paths in Web Development
content: When working on a website, you'll frequently encounter symbols such as /, ./, and ../ in file paths. They may look similar, but each one tells your browser or development environment something different about where to find a file.
What is the difference? When should you use each one?
Understanding these symbols makes it easier to organize website files, link CSS stylesheets, load images, import JavaScript modules, and navigate project folders without getting lost.
Let's break them down with practical examples.
Here are the most common symbols and URL patterns you'll encounter in web development.

SymbolMeaningTypical use
/Website root (when used as a root-relative URL)Access files from the site root
./Current directoryReference files relative to the current location
../Parent directory (one level up)Access files in the folder above
../../Two levels upNavigate to a higher-level folder
https://Full URL with protocolLink to an external website or resource
#Fragment identifierJump to a specific section on a page
?Begins a query stringPass parameters through a URL
A forward slash at the beginning of a URL path means you're starting from the website's root path.
This tells the browser to look for the image at:
It doesn't matter whether the current page is:
The path /images/logo.png still points to the same location on that website.

• Loading images stored in a root-level images folder.
  • Referencing files that should have the same URL regardless of the current page's location.
  • Linking to root-level pages or resources.
Remember: A leading / refers to the website's root URL path, not necessarily the root of your computer's file system.
It tells the browser or module resolver to look for a file relative to the current location.
For example, suppose you have this folder structure:
Inside index.html, you can reference the stylesheet like this:

1. Start from the directory containing index.html.
  2. Open the css folder.
  3. Find style.css.
Both paths resolve to the same location in this example.

• Referencing files relative to the current directory.
  • Linking CSS, images, and other resources.
  • Importing local modules in JavaScript.
The symbol ../ means go up one directory level to the parent folder.
But the image you want is located in the parent directory's images folder.

1. ../ moves up from pages to my-website.
  2. images/ enters the images folder.
  3. logo.png identifies the image file.

• Accessing files in a parent directory.
  • Referencing shared resources from nested folders.
  • Importing modules located outside the current folder.
What if the file you need is even farther away?
You can repeat ../ to move up multiple directory levels.

my-website/
├── index.html
├── images/
│   └── logo.png
└── pages/
    └── articles/
        └── article.html
To access logo.png, you need to move up two levels:

1. First ../ moves from articles to pages.
  2. Second ../ moves from pages to my-website.
  3. images/ enters the images folder.
  4. logo.png identifies the file.

• ../ = Go up one level.
  • ../../ = Go up two levels.
  • ../../../ = Go up three levels.
Each additional ../ moves one more directory level upward.
Unlike relative paths, https:// starts a complete URL that identifies a resource on a particular domain.

• Linking to external websites.
  • Loading images hosted on another domain.
  • Referencing externally hosted resources.
Unlike /, ./, and ../, a complete URL doesn't depend on the current page's directory.
The # symbol identifies a fragment within a page.
The link points to an element with the matching ID:
When someone clicks the link, the browser navigates to that section.
You can also use a fragment to link to a section on another page:
The question mark begins a query string.

• ? starts the query string.
  • page is the parameter name.
  • 2 is its value.
Query strings are commonly used for pagination, search terms, filters, and other URL-based settings.
9. Practical Example: Understanding Paths in a Website Project
Imagine your website has this folder structure:

my-website/
│
├── index.html
│
├── css/
│   └── style.css
│
├── images/
│   ├── logo.png
│   └── banner.jpg
│
└── pages/
    ├── about.html
    │
    └── articles/
        └── article.html
Assume you're working inside index.html, which is located directly in the project root.

PathWhere it points
./css/style.csscss/style.css relative to the current directory
css/style.cssThe same stylesheet
/images/logo.pngimages/logo.png from the website root
./images/banner.jpgimages/banner.jpg relative to the current directory
Your paths change depending on where the target files are located:

PathWhere it points
./article.htmlThe current article file
../about.htmlpages/about.html
../../index.htmlThe root index.html
../../images/logo.pngThe root images/logo.png file
Notice how the same file can require a different relative path depending on where the current file is located.
That's the key to understanding relative paths.
10. Important Distinction: URL Paths vs. File System Paths
One detail worth remembering is that / does not always refer to the same root.
The leading slash means the root path of the website's domain.
Represents the root of the entire file system.
These are different concepts, even though they use the same symbol.
Also, in web development, relative URL paths and JavaScript module imports can follow different resolution rules depending on how they're used.

• An HTML image path is generally resolved relative to the document's URL.
  • A JavaScript module import such as import "./utils.js" is resolved relative to the importing module.
  • A root-relative URL beginning with / is resolved against the URL origin's root path.
Understanding what the path is relative to is just as important as understanding the symbols themselves.

SymbolEasy way to remember
/Start from the website root
./Stay in the current directory
../Go up one directory
../../Go up two directories
https://Use a complete URL
#Jump to a section
?Pass URL parameters
When working with website files, remember these three essential symbols:

• / starts from the website's root path.
  • ./ starts from the current directory.
  • ../ moves up one directory level.
If you understand these three symbols, navigating project folders and referencing resources becomes much easier.
A simple rule to remember: / starts at the root, ./ stays here, and ../ goes up.
